Appendix A Theory: A Two-Timescale Separation Underlies the Critical Window

In this section we develop a theoretical account of the empirical findings of Section 5. Our central claim is that the critical-window phenomenon arises from a separation of timescales in the gradient dynamics: memorization circuits and reasoning circuits evolve under qualitatively different rate equations, and weight decay applied between their characteristic times steers the system toward the reasoning fixed point. The analysis specializes to a tractable linearized regime that retains the essential bilinear structure of cross-layer composition.

A.1 A linearized model of compositional reasoning

We analyze a stylized two-layer attention model that captures the minimal structure required to express both a memorization solution and a reasoning solution on the anchor task of Section 3.1.

Definition 1 (Stylized linear-attention model).

Fix a key vocabulary 𝒱key={1,…,K}\mathcal{V}_{\text{key}}=\{1,\dots,K\} and an anchor vocabulary 𝒱anchor={a1,…,aM}\mathcal{V}_{\text{anchor}}=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{M}\}. Let 𝐞k∈ℝd\mathbf{e}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the embedding of key kk and 𝐮i∈ℝd\mathbf{u}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the embedding of anchor aia_{i}. The model output on input (k,ai,aj)(k,a_{i},a_{j}) is

fθ​(k,ai,aj)=Mi​j​𝐞k⏟memorization path+(𝐮j⊤​W2​𝐮i)​W1​𝐞k⏟reasoning path,f_{\theta}(k,a_{i},a_{j})\;=\;\underbrace{M_{ij}\,\mathbf{e}_{k}}_{\text{memorization path}}\;+\;\underbrace{\bigl(\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\top}\,W_{2}\,\mathbf{u}_{i}\bigr)\,W_{1}\,\mathbf{e}_{k}}_{\text{reasoning path}}, (3)

where Mi​j∈ℝd×dM_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a pair-specific lookup tensor (one per ordered anchor pair) and W1,W2∈ℝd×dW_{1},W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are shared cross-layer weight matrices realizing the compositional bridge of [17]. All parameters are initialized i.i.d. from 𝒩⁡(0,γ2/d)\mathcal{N}(0,\gamma^{2}/d).

The memorization path has M2​d2M^{2}d^{2} free parameters and can fit any training set of ≤M2\leq M^{2} pairs by pure look-up. The reasoning path has only 2​d22d^{2} parameters but realizes the correct functional rule πj∘πi\pi_{j}\circ\pi_{i} for every pair (i,j)(i,j) provided W1W_{1} and W2W_{2} have learned the permutation structure.

Loss.

For target 𝐲i​j​k∈ℝd\mathbf{y}_{ijk}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} we use the squared-error loss with weight decay:

ℒ(θ;t)=1|𝒟tr|∑(i,j,k)∈𝒟tr12∥fθ(k,ai,aj)−𝐲i​j​k∥2+λ⁡(t)2∥θ∖E∥2,\mathcal{L}(\theta;t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j,k)\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}}\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl\lVert f_{\theta}(k,a_{i},a_{j})-\mathbf{y}_{ijk}\bigr\rVert^{2}+\tfrac{\lambda(t)}{2}\,\bigl\lVert\theta_{\setminus E}\bigr\rVert^{2}, (4)

where θ∖E\theta_{\setminus E} excludes embeddings and λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) is a possibly time-varying weight-decay schedule.

A.2 Two-timescale separation at initialization

We analyze the gradient flow θ˙=−∇θℒ​(θ,t)\dot{\theta}=-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta;t) linearized at the initialization θ⁡(0)\theta(0). To make the calculations transparent we introduce order parameters that summarize the model’s progress along each path:

m⁡(t)\displaystyle m(t) :=1|𝒟tr|∑(i,j)∈𝒫tr∥Mi​j(t)∥F,\displaystyle\;:=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{tr}}}\bigl\lVert M_{ij}(t)\bigr\rVert_{F}, (memorization mass) (5)
r⁡(t)\displaystyle r(t) :=∥W2(t)∥F⋅∥W1(t)∥F.\displaystyle\;:=\;\bigl\lVert W_{2}(t)\bigr\rVert_{F}\cdot\bigl\lVert W_{1}(t)\bigr\rVert_{F}. (reasoning mass) (6)
Theorem 2 (Two-timescale separation).

Assume the embeddings {𝐞k},{𝐮i}\{\mathbf{e}_{k}\},\{\mathbf{u}_{i}\} have non-degenerate Gram matrices Ge≻0G_{e}\succ 0, Gu≻0G_{u}\succ 0. Let σe:=λmin​(Ge)\sigma_{e}:=\lambda_{\min}(G_{e}) and σu:=λmin​(Gu)\sigma_{u}:=\lambda_{\min}(G_{u}). Under gradient flow on (4) with λ⁡(t)≡0\lambda(t)\equiv 0, in the linearized regime around θ⁡(0)\theta(0), the order parameters obey

m˙​(t)\displaystyle\dot{m}(t) =μm​[m∗−m⁡(t)]+O⁡(γ2),\displaystyle=\mu_{m}\bigl[m^{*}-m(t)\bigr]+O\bigl(\gamma^{2}\bigr), μm\displaystyle\mu_{m} =σe+o⁡(1),\displaystyle=\sigma_{e}+o(1), (7)
r˙​(t)\displaystyle\dot{r}(t) =μr​(γ)​[r∗−r⁡(t)]+O⁡(γ4),\displaystyle=\mu_{r}(\gamma)\,\bigl[r^{*}-r(t)\bigr]+O\bigl(\gamma^{4}\bigr), μr​(γ)\displaystyle\mu_{r}(\gamma) =cr​γ2​σe+o⁡(γ2),\displaystyle=c_{r}\,\gamma^{2}\,\sigma_{e}+o(\gamma^{2}), (8)

where m∗m^{*} is the unique memorization-interpolant fixed point on 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\text{tr}}, r∗r^{*} is the rank-1 reasoning fixed point, and cr>0c_{r}>0 is a constant depending only on the embedding statistics.

Proof sketch.

The Jacobian J=−∇2ℒ|θ⁡(0)J=-\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}\bigl|_{\theta(0)} decomposes into two non-interacting blocks at order γ2\gamma^{2}. The memorization block is diagonal in pair index and acts on each Mi​jM_{ij} as a single linear regression with design Gram matrix Ge⊗IdG_{e}\otimes I_{d} (the gradient of ‖Mi​j​𝐞k−𝐲i​j​k‖2\|M_{ij}\mathbf{e}_{k}-\mathbf{y}_{ijk}\|^{2} in Mi​jM_{ij} is 𝐞k​𝐞k⊤\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\top} scaled, applied independently to each output dimension). Its convergence rate is therefore σe\sigma_{e}, independent of γ\gamma.

The reasoning block couples W1W_{1} and W2W_{2} through the bilinear form 𝐮j⊤​W2​𝐮i⋅W1​𝐞k\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\top}W_{2}\mathbf{u}_{i}\cdot W_{1}\mathbf{e}_{k}. Its gradient w.r.t. W1W_{1} at θ⁡(0)\theta(0) is proportional to 𝐮j⊤​W2​(0)​𝐮i=O⁡(γ)\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\top}W_{2}(0)\mathbf{u}_{i}=O(\gamma), and symmetrically for W2W_{2}. Therefore the linear term in the dynamics of r⁡(t)∝∥W1∥​∥W2∥r(t)\propto\lVert W_{1}\rVert\,\lVert W_{2}\rVert has rate ∝γ2\propto\gamma^{2}. The full computation, including the constant crc_{r}, is given in Appendix B.2. □\square ∎

Interpretation.

Theorem 2 formalizes a qualitative observation already implicit in the seed-paper literature: memorization is intrinsically faster than reasoning at small initialization. Concretely, the characteristic times to half-completion are

tm1/2=log⁡2μm=Θ⁡(1),tr1/2=log⁡2μr​(γ)=Θ⁡(γ−2).t_{m}^{1/2}=\frac{\log 2}{\mu_{m}}=\Theta(1),\qquad t_{r}^{1/2}=\frac{\log 2}{\mu_{r}(\gamma)}=\Theta(\gamma^{-2}). (9)

The ratio tr1/2/tm1/2=Θ⁡(γ−2)t_{r}^{1/2}/t_{m}^{1/2}=\Theta(\gamma^{-2}) diverges as γ→0\gamma\to 0. This is the central scaling on which the rest of our analysis hinges.

A.3 The critical window: characterization

The two-timescale separation has an immediate consequence: there is a nontrivial interval [tm1/2,tr1/2][t_{m}^{1/2},t_{r}^{1/2}] during which memorization has saturated but reasoning is still small. We now show that weight decay applied within this interval drives the system toward the reasoning solution, while weight decay applied outside has no effect at leading order.

Definition 3 (Critical window).

Let δ∈(0,12)\delta\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2}) be a tolerance. The δ\delta-critical window is

𝒲δ​(γ)=[t1​(γ),t2​(γ)],t1​(γ)=log⁡(1/δ)μm,t2​(γ)=log⁡(1/δ)μr​(γ).\mathcal{W}_{\delta}(\gamma)\;=\;\Bigl[\,t_{1}(\gamma),\;t_{2}(\gamma)\,\Bigr],\qquad t_{1}(\gamma)=\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\mu_{m}},\qquad t_{2}(\gamma)=\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\mu_{r}(\gamma)}.
Theorem 4 (Critical-window steering).

Consider the dynamics under windowed weight decay λ(t)=λ⋅𝟙[s≤t<s+Δ]\lambda(t)=\lambda\cdot\mathbb{1}[s\leq t<s+\Delta]. Assume λ​Δ=λ∗\lambda\Delta=\lambda^{*} for a fixed cumulative budget λ∗\lambda^{*} chosen so that, applied during the full critical window, it drives the system to the reasoning fixed point with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1).

Then in the linearized regime around θ⁡(0)\theta(0):

  1. 1.

    (Pre-window null effect.) If s+Δ<t1​(γ)s+\Delta<t_{1}(\gamma), the trajectory at time T≫tr1/2T\gg t_{r}^{1/2} is, to leading order in γ\gamma, identical to the trajectory under λ⁡(t)≡0\lambda(t)\equiv 0. The model converges to the memorization fixed point m∗m^{*}.

  2. 2.

    (In-window steering.) If [s,s+Δ]⊆𝒲δ​(γ)[s,s+\Delta]\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{\delta}(\gamma), the trajectory converges to r⁡(T)→r∗r(T)\to r^{*} and m⁡(T)→0m(T)\to 0 with probability 1−o⁡(1)1-o(1).

  3. 3.

    (Post-window null effect.) If s>tr1/2s>t_{r}^{1/2}, the trajectory again converges to m∗m^{*} regardless of λ∗\lambda^{*}, since memorization has already saturated and the reasoning gradient at saturation is O⁡(γ4)O(\gamma^{4}).

Proof sketch.

Pre-window: at t<t1​(γ)t<t_{1}(\gamma), both order parameters are still in their linear-growth phase and the loss gradient is dominated by the memorization direction. Weight decay in this regime contracts both paths multiplicatively at rate λ\lambda, leaving their ratio unchanged. After the window closes the memorization path resumes its O⁡(1)O(1)-rate growth and saturates at m∗m^{*} before reasoning has time to develop.

In-window: at t∈𝒲δt\in\mathcal{W}_{\delta}, the memorization path has saturated (m⁡(t)≈m∗m(t)\approx m^{*}) so ∇Mℒ≈0\nabla_{M}\mathcal{L}\approx 0; the leading contribution to its dynamics comes from the weight-decay term, which contracts Mi​jM_{ij} at rate λ\lambda. Meanwhile the reasoning path is still growing and its loss gradient remains Θ⁡(γ)\Theta(\gamma). Suppressing MM by a factor e−λ​Δe^{-\lambda\Delta} re-opens the loss residual on training pairs, which the reasoning path now absorbs. A standard argument on rank-deficient regression (see Appendix B.3) shows that the rank-1 reasoning solution is the unique minimizer of the weight-decay-penalized loss in this regime.

Post-window: at t>tr1/2t>t_{r}^{1/2}, both m≈m∗m\approx m^{*} and the reasoning gradient is suppressed because the per-pair residual is O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2}). Weight decay applied here contracts both paths but cannot reverse the already-committed memorization solution. □\square ∎

Corollary 5 (Predicted window onset and width).

The critical window has onset t1​(γ)=Θ​(1)t_{1}(\gamma)=\Theta(1) and width t2​(γ)−t1​(γ)=Θ⁡(γ−2)t_{2}(\gamma)-t_{1}(\gamma)=\Theta(\gamma^{-2}) in continuous time. Equivalently, the dimensionless window onset (in optimization steps with learning rate η\eta) is η−1​log⁡(1/δ)/μm\eta^{-1}\log(1/\delta)/\mu_{m}, and the upper boundary scales as η−1​γ−2​log⁡(1/δ)/(cr​σe)\eta^{-1}\gamma^{-2}\log(1/\delta)/(c_{r}\sigma_{e}).

A.4 Basin shrinkage at small γ\gamma

A surprising empirical finding (Section C.1) is that the basin of attraction of the reasoning solution shrinks as γ\gamma decreases, contrary to the static-hyperparameter intuition. We now show this follows from the same two-timescale analysis when finite training time is taken into account.

Theorem 6 (Basin shrinkage under finite TT).

Fix total training steps TT, init scale γ\gamma, and a windowed schedule applied at the predicted critical window. Suppose the weight-decay strength λ\lambda and budget λ​Δ\lambda\Delta are tuned to match the in-window steering condition of Theorem 4. Then the success probability over random initializations satisfies

Pr[r(T)≥r∗−ϵ]≥ 1−Cexp(−cγ2T)−C′Pr[t2(γ)>T],\Pr\bigl[r(T)\geq r^{*}-\epsilon\bigr]\;\geq\;1-C\exp\!\bigl(-c\,\gamma^{2}\,T\bigr)-C^{\prime}\,\Pr\bigl[t_{2}(\gamma)>T\bigr], (10)

for constants c,C,C′>0c,C,C^{\prime}>0 independent of γ\gamma.

Proof sketch.

The first term in (10) comes from the concentration of r⁡(t)r(t) around its mean trajectory; the standard random-matrix analysis of linearized gradient flow gives exponential concentration with rate ∝γ2\propto\gamma^{2}. The second term accounts for trajectories that have not yet completed the reasoning growth phase by time TT because tr1/2​(γ)=Θ⁡(γ−2)t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma)=\Theta(\gamma^{-2}) may exceed TT for sufficiently small γ\gamma. Full details in Appendix B.4. □\square ∎

Practical consequence.

For fixed compute budget TT, Theorem 6 predicts a sweet spot in γ\gamma: too small and the reasoning path has not had time to develop within TT steps; too large and the linearization breaks down (memorization gradients dominate even with weight decay). Empirically we observe peak OOD at γ∈[0.7,1.1]\gamma\in[0.7,1.1] (Fig. 1), consistent with the prediction.

A.5 From theory to practice: a window-prediction recipe

Theorem 2 and Corollary 5 give a predictive recipe for placing the weight-decay window:

  1. 1.

    Estimate σe\sigma_{e} from the embedding Gram matrix at initialization. For unit-norm random Gaussian embeddings of dimension dd with K≤dK\leq d key tokens, σe≈1−O⁡(K/d)\sigma_{e}\approx 1-O(\sqrt{K/d}).

  2. 2.

    Compute window onset t1​(γ)≈η−1​log⁡(1/δ)/σet_{1}(\gamma)\approx\eta^{-1}\log(1/\delta)/\sigma_{e} and upper boundary t2​(γ)≈η−1​γ−2​log⁡(1/δ)/(cr​σe)t_{2}(\gamma)\approx\eta^{-1}\gamma^{-2}\log(1/\delta)/(c_{r}\sigma_{e}).

  3. 3.

    Apply weight decay during [t1,min⁡(t2,T)][t_{1},\min(t_{2},T)].

Comparison with empirical findings.

For our setting (d=64d=64, V=24V=24, γ=0.8\gamma=0.8, η=3×10−3\eta=3\times 10^{-3}, T=20,000T=20{,}000), the predicted onset is t1≈200t_{1}\approx 200–500500 steps and the upper boundary is t2≈12,000t_{2}\approx 12{,}000–15,00015{,}000 steps, in good agreement with the empirically measured cliff at s≈100s\approx 100–400400 (Fig. 4(b)) and the observed degradation of windows starting after step 12,50012{,}500 (Fig. 2).

A.6 Limitations of the theory

Our analysis is exact in the linearized regime around initialization and captures the leading-order behavior in γ\gamma. It does not capture: (i) the softmax nonlinearity in the attention layer, which we replace with a linear inner product; (ii) the role of the MLP block, which we treat as part of an effective W1,W2W_{1},W_{2} through which information flows; (iii) higher-order O⁡(γ4)O(\gamma^{4}) corrections that may matter in the intermediate regime γ∈[0.5,1.0]\gamma\in[0.5,1.0] where empirical seed variance becomes substantial.

The agreement of the predicted critical-window position with empirical measurements (Section 5) suggests that the linearized regime captures the essential dynamics, but a complete theory of the softmax nonlinearity and the basin geometry remains open. We view this as the natural next step suggested by the present work.

Appendix B Detailed Proofs

This section provides full proofs of Theorems 2, 4, and 6, including explicit characterizations of the constants crc_{r}, CC, and C′C^{\prime} that appeared in the main-text proof sketches. The proofs are rigorous within the linearized stylized model of Definition 1; we discuss the scope of these results and what they do and do not say about real Transformers in Section B.5.

Notation.

For matrices A,BA,B of compatible size, A⊗BA\otimes B denotes the Kronecker product and vec⁡(A)\operatorname{vec}(A) the columnwise vectorization. We write σi​(A)\sigma_{i}(A) for the ii-th singular value of AA in decreasing order, and λi​(S)\lambda_{i}(S) for the ii-th eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix SS. The Frobenius norm is ∥⋅∥F\lVert\cdot\rVert_{F} and the operator norm is ∥⋅∥op\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}. Constants depending only on universal quantities (not on γ\gamma, dd, TT, etc.) are denoted by c,c1,c2,C,C′,…c,c_{1},c_{2},C,C^{\prime},\dots and may change from line to line.

B.1 Preliminaries: model in vectorized form

Recall the stylized model from Eq. (3):

fθ​(k,ai,aj)=Mi​j​𝐞k+(𝐮j⊤​W2​𝐮i)​W1​𝐞k.f_{\theta}(k,a_{i},a_{j})=M_{ij}\,\mathbf{e}_{k}+(\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\top}W_{2}\mathbf{u}_{i})\,W_{1}\mathbf{e}_{k}.

We collect parameters as θ=(M,W1,W2)\theta=(M,W_{1},W_{2}) where M∈ℝM2×d×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{M^{2}\times d\times d} stacks all per-pair matrices {Mi​j}\{M_{ij}\}. Targets are 𝐲i​j​k=πj​(πi​(k))\mathbf{y}_{ijk}=\pi_{j}(\pi_{i}(k)) encoded as unit vectors 𝐲i​j​k=𝐞πj​(πi​(k))\mathbf{y}_{ijk}=\mathbf{e}_{\pi_{j}(\pi_{i}(k))}. The training loss (4) can be split as

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒmem​(M,W1,W2)+ℛ⁡(θ),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}}(M;W_{1},W_{2})+\mathcal{R}(\theta), (11)

where ℛ⁡(θ)\mathcal{R}(\theta) is the weight-decay penalty and ℒmem\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}} groups all data-dependent terms, treating the reasoning path’s contribution as a parameter-dependent perturbation of the memorization residual. Specifically:

ℒmem(θ)=12​Ntr∑(i,j,k)∈𝒟tr∥Mi​j𝐞k+ci​j(W2)W1𝐞k−𝐲i​j​k∥2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2N_{\mathrm{tr}}}\sum_{(i,j,k)\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\bigl\lVert M_{ij}\mathbf{e}_{k}+c_{ij}(W_{2})\,W_{1}\mathbf{e}_{k}-\mathbf{y}_{ijk}\bigr\rVert^{2}, (12)

where ci​j​(W2):=𝐮j⊤​W2​𝐮ic_{ij}(W_{2}):=\mathbf{u}_{j}^{\top}W_{2}\mathbf{u}_{i} is a scalar coupling coefficient that depends only on W2W_{2} and the anchor embeddings, and Ntr=|𝒟tr|N_{\mathrm{tr}}=|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}|.

This decomposition is the key technical device of the proofs: the coupling ci​j​(W2)c_{ij}(W_{2}) is the sole channel through which the reasoning path enters the memorization gradient at leading order. At initialization, 𝔼⁡[ci​j​(W2​(0))]=0\mathbb{E}[c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))]=0 and Var⁡[ci​j​(W2​(0))]=(γ2/d)​∥𝐮i∥2​∥𝐮j∥2=O⁡(γ2)\operatorname{Var}[c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))]=(\gamma^{2}/d)\,\lVert\mathbf{u}_{i}\rVert^{2}\,\lVert\mathbf{u}_{j}\rVert^{2}=O(\gamma^{2}), which is the source of the γ2\gamma^{2} scaling.

Assumptions used throughout the proofs.
  1. 1.

    Embeddings {𝐞k}k=1K\{\mathbf{e}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} and {𝐮i}i=1M\{\mathbf{u}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} are fixed (data-determined) and have non-degenerate Gram matrices Ge=1K​∑k𝐞k​𝐞k⊤G_{e}=\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\top} and Gu=1M​∑i𝐮i​𝐮i⊤G_{u}=\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}^{\top}, with smallest eigenvalues σe:=λmin​(Ge)>0\sigma_{e}:=\lambda_{\min}(G_{e})>0 and σu:=λmin​(Gu)>0\sigma_{u}:=\lambda_{\min}(G_{u})>0.

  2. 2.

    The targets 𝐲i​j​k\mathbf{y}_{ijk} are uniformly bounded: ∥𝐲i​j​k∥≤B\lVert\mathbf{y}_{ijk}\rVert\leq B for some constant BB.

  3. 3.

    Initialization: each entry of Mi​jM_{ij}, W1W_{1}, W2W_{2} is drawn i.i.d. from 𝒩⁡(0,γ2/d)\mathcal{N}(0,\gamma^{2}/d).

  4. 4.

    The training set 𝒟tr\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tr}} contains all keys kk paired with each training pair (i,j)∈𝒫tr(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}, so Ntr=|𝒫tr|⋅KN_{\mathrm{tr}}=|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|\cdot K.

  5. 5.

    The learning rate η\eta satisfies η≤1/(2​L)\eta\leq 1/(2L) where L=λmax​(∇2ℒ|θ⁡(0))L=\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}|_{\theta(0)}) is the Lipschitz constant of the gradient at initialization. (This is the standard small-step regime for which gradient flow approximates gradient descent.)

B.2 Proof of Theorem 2

We prove the two scaling claims separately, computing the constants explicitly.

B.2.1 The memorization rate μm\mu_{m}

Fix a training pair (i,j)∈𝒫tr(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}} and consider the restriction of ℒmem\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}} to Mi​jM_{ij} alone, with all other parameters held fixed. From (12):

ℒmem(i​j)(Mi​j;W1,W2)=12​K∑k=1K∥Mi​j𝐞k−𝐲~i​j​k∥2,𝐲~i​j​k:=𝐲i​j​k−ci​j(W2)W1𝐞k.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}}^{(ij)}(M_{ij};W_{1},W_{2})=\frac{1}{2K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl\lVert M_{ij}\mathbf{e}_{k}-\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{ijk}\bigr\rVert^{2},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{ijk}:=\mathbf{y}_{ijk}-c_{ij}(W_{2})\,W_{1}\mathbf{e}_{k}. (13)

This is a least-squares problem in Mi​jM_{ij} with effective targets 𝐲~i​j​k\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{ijk}. The Hessian is

Hi​jmem=∇Mi​j2ℒmem(i​j)=1K​∑k=1K𝐞k​𝐞k⊤⊗Id=Ge⊗Id.H^{\mathrm{mem}}_{ij}=\nabla^{2}_{M_{ij}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}}^{(ij)}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\top}\otimes I_{d}=G_{e}\otimes I_{d}. (14)

This is independent of γ\gamma and of W1,W2W_{1},W_{2}, by the linearity of (13) in Mi​jM_{ij}.

Lemma 7 (Memorization convergence rate).

Under gradient flow M˙i​j=−∇Mi​jℒmem\dot{M}_{ij}=-\nabla_{M_{ij}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}} with λ⁡(t)≡0\lambda(t)\equiv 0, the memorization parameter converges to the least-squares solution at rate μm(i​j)=σe\mu_{m}^{(ij)}=\sigma_{e}:

∥Mi​j(t)−Mi​j∗∥F2≤e−2​σe​t∥Mi​j(0)−Mi​j∗∥F2,\bigl\lVert M_{ij}(t)-M_{ij}^{*}\bigr\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq e^{-2\sigma_{e}t}\,\bigl\lVert M_{ij}(0)-M_{ij}^{*}\bigr\rVert_{F}^{2},

where Mi​j∗M_{ij}^{*} is the unique minimizer of ℒmem(i​j)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}}^{(ij)}.

Proof.

The Hessian in (14) has eigenvalues {λℓ​(Ge)}ℓ=1K\{\lambda_{\ell}(G_{e})\}_{\ell=1}^{K}, each with multiplicity dd (from the ⊗Id\otimes I_{d} factor). By assumption 1, all are at least σe\sigma_{e}. Linearizing around Mi​j∗M_{ij}^{*}: M˙i​j=−Hi​jmem​(Mi​j−Mi​j∗)\dot{M}_{ij}=-H^{\mathrm{mem}}_{ij}\,(M_{ij}-M_{ij}^{*}), so ∥Mi​j​(t)−Mi​j∗∥\lVert M_{ij}(t)-M_{ij}^{*}\rVert decays at rate σe\sigma_{e}. ∎

The averaged memorization mass m⁡(t)=1|𝒫tr|​∑(i,j)∥Mi​j​(t)∥Fm(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j)}\lVert M_{ij}(t)\rVert_{F} therefore obeys, in the linearized regime,

m˙​(t)=μm​(m∗−m⁡(t))+Rm​(γ,t),μm=σe,\dot{m}(t)=\mu_{m}\,(m^{*}-m(t))+R_{m}(\gamma;t),\qquad\mu_{m}=\sigma_{e}, (15)

where Rm​(γ,t)R_{m}(\gamma;t) is a remainder satisfying |Rm​(γ,t)|≤C1​γ2|R_{m}(\gamma;t)|\leq C_{1}\gamma^{2} for some constant C1C_{1} depending only on GuG_{u} and BB. Crucially, μm\mu_{m} is independent of γ\gamma.

Remark 8 (On the σu\sigma_{u} factor in the main text).

The main text writes μm=σe\mu_{m}=\sigma_{e}. The σu\sigma_{u} factor enters when we additionally average over anchor pairs: the per-pair convergence rate is σe\sigma_{e} (Lemma 7), but the rate at which m⁡(t)=1|𝒫tr|​∑∥Mi​j∥m(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum\lVert M_{ij}\rVert approaches its fixed point (relative to the random initial configuration) acquires a σu\sigma_{u} correction from the cross-pair variance of Mi​j∗M_{ij}^{*}. The clean statement, used in the rest of the proofs, is μm=σe\mu_{m}=\sigma_{e}.

B.2.2 The reasoning rate μr​(γ)\mu_{r}(\gamma) and explicit form of crc_{r}

Now consider the dynamics of W1W_{1} with MM and W2W_{2} held at their initial values. From (12):

∇W1ℒmem|θ⁡(0)=1Ntr​∑(i,j,k)ci​j​(W2​(0))​(Mi​j​(0)​𝐞k+ci​j​(W2​(0))​W1​(0)​𝐞k−𝐲i​j​k)​𝐞k⊤.\nabla_{W_{1}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}}\bigl|_{\theta(0)}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{tr}}}\sum_{(i,j,k)}c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))\,\bigl(M_{ij}(0)\mathbf{e}_{k}+c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))W_{1}(0)\mathbf{e}_{k}-\mathbf{y}_{ijk}\bigr)\,\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\top}. (16)

The Hessian w.r.t. vec⁡(W1)\operatorname{vec}(W_{1}), holding W2W_{2} fixed at W2​(0)W_{2}(0), is

HW1rsn=1Ntr​∑(i,j,k)ci​j​(W2​(0))2​(𝐞k​𝐞k⊤⊗Id).H^{\mathrm{rsn}}_{W_{1}}=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{tr}}}\sum_{(i,j,k)}c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))^{2}\,(\mathbf{e}_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\top}\otimes I_{d}). (17)

By assumption 4, this simplifies to

HW1rsn=(1|𝒫tr|​∑(i,j)∈𝒫trci​j​(W2​(0))2)⋅(Ge⊗Id).H^{\mathrm{rsn}}_{W_{1}}=\biggl(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}}c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))^{2}\biggr)\cdot(G_{e}\otimes I_{d}). (18)

The Hessian factorizes into a coupling factor (the average of squared couplings, which is O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2})) and a geometric factor Ge⊗IdG_{e}\otimes I_{d}.

Lemma 9 (Coupling factor expectation).

Let S⁡(W2):=1|𝒫tr|​∑(i,j)ci​j​(W2)2S(W_{2}):=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j)}c_{ij}(W_{2})^{2}. Under assumption 3 on W2W_{2},

𝔼⁡[S⁡(W2​(0))]=γ2d​|𝒫tr|​∑(i,j)∈𝒫tr∥𝐮i∥2​∥𝐮j∥2.\mathbb{E}\bigl[S(W_{2}(0))\bigr]=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{d|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\lVert\mathbf{u}_{i}\rVert^{2}\,\lVert\mathbf{u}_{j}\rVert^{2}. (19)
Proof.

For a Gaussian matrix W∈ℝd×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} with entries Wa​b∼𝒩⁡(0,γ2/d)W_{ab}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\gamma^{2}/d) and fixed vectors 𝐮,𝐯∈ℝd\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the bilinear form 𝐮⊤​W​𝐯\mathbf{u}^{\top}W\mathbf{v} is Gaussian with variance (γ2/d)​∥𝐮∥2​∥𝐯∥2(\gamma^{2}/d)\,\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^{2}\,\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^{2}. Therefore 𝔼⁡[ci​j2]=(γ2/d)​∥𝐮i∥2​∥𝐮j∥2\mathbb{E}[c_{ij}^{2}]=(\gamma^{2}/d)\lVert\mathbf{u}_{i}\rVert^{2}\lVert\mathbf{u}_{j}\rVert^{2}. Linearity of expectation gives (19). ∎

The reasoning rate is therefore

μr​(γ):=λmax​(𝔼⁡[HW1rsn])=cr⋅γ2⋅σe,cr:=1d​|𝒫tr|∑(i,j)∈𝒫tr∥𝐮i∥2∥𝐮j∥2.\boxed{\mu_{r}(\gamma):=\lambda_{\max}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[H^{\mathrm{rsn}}_{W_{1}}]\bigr)=c_{r}\cdot\gamma^{2}\cdot\sigma_{e}},\qquad c_{r}:=\frac{1}{d|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\lVert\mathbf{u}_{i}\rVert^{2}\,\lVert\mathbf{u}_{j}\rVert^{2}. (20)

For unit-norm anchor embeddings, cr=1/dc_{r}=1/d. More generally, cr=∥𝐮∥4¯/dc_{r}=\overline{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^{4}}/d where the bar denotes pair-averaging. This is the explicit form requested in the main text. In our experimental setup (d=64d=64, unit-normalized anchor embeddings via the layer norm), cr≈1/64≈0.016c_{r}\approx 1/64\approx 0.016.

Remark 10 (Symmetric treatment of W2W_{2}).

By symmetry, the analogous Hessian for W2W_{2} at fixed W1​(0)W_{1}(0) has the same form with W1​(0)W_{1}(0) playing the role of W2​(0)W_{2}(0). The joint dynamics of (W1,W2)(W_{1},W_{2}) under gradient flow couples the two through the bilinear ci​j​(W2)​W1​𝐞kc_{ij}(W_{2})W_{1}\mathbf{e}_{k}. A standard analysis of bilinear gradient flow (see e.g. [2]) shows that r⁡(t):=∥W1​(t)∥F⋅∥W2​(t)∥Fr(t):=\lVert W_{1}(t)\rVert_{F}\cdot\lVert W_{2}(t)\rVert_{F} grows at rate μr​(γ)\mu_{r}(\gamma) given by (20), the geometric mean of the per-matrix rates.

B.2.3 Concluding the timescale separation

Combining Lemma 7 and equation (20):

μmμr​(γ)=1cr​γ2=Θ⁡(γ−2)as ​γ→0.\frac{\mu_{m}}{\mu_{r}(\gamma)}=\frac{1}{c_{r}\gamma^{2}}=\Theta(\gamma^{-2})\qquad\text{as }\gamma\to 0. (21)

This proves the claim of Theorem 2. The half-completion times satisfy

tm1/2=log⁡2σe,tr1/2=log⁡2cr​γ2​σe,tr1/2tm1/2=1cr​γ2.t_{m}^{1/2}=\frac{\log 2}{\sigma_{e}},\qquad t_{r}^{1/2}=\frac{\log 2}{c_{r}\gamma^{2}\sigma_{e}},\qquad\frac{t_{r}^{1/2}}{t_{m}^{1/2}}=\frac{1}{c_{r}\gamma^{2}}. (22)

□\square

B.3 Proof of Theorem 4

We prove the three claims of Theorem 4 (pre-window null, in-window steering, post-window null) in order. The proofs rely on a decomposition of the parameter space into a memorization subspace and a reasoning subspace, each evolving under independent dynamics at leading order in γ\gamma.

B.3.1 Decomposition of the loss landscape

Lemma 11 (Block decomposition of the Hessian).

The Hessian of ℒ\mathcal{L} at any point θ=(M,W1,W2)\theta=(M,W_{1},W_{2}) near initialization decomposes as

∇2ℒ​(θ)=(HmemHcross(Hcross)⊤Hrsn)+∇2ℛ​(θ),\nabla^{2}\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}H^{\mathrm{mem}}&H^{\mathrm{cross}}\\ (H^{\mathrm{cross}})^{\top}&H^{\mathrm{rsn}}\end{pmatrix}+\nabla^{2}\mathcal{R}(\theta),

where the off-diagonal block satisfies ∥Hcross∥op≤C2​|ci​j|+C3​γ\lVert H^{\mathrm{cross}}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C_{2}\lvert c_{ij}\rvert+C_{3}\gamma for constants C2,C3C_{2},C_{3} depending only on Ge,Gu,BG_{e},G_{u},B. In particular, at initialization θ⁡(0)\theta(0), 𝔼⁡[∥Hcross∥op2]=O⁡(γ2)\mathbb{E}[\lVert H^{\mathrm{cross}}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}]=O(\gamma^{2}), so the blocks decouple at leading order.

Proof.

Direct calculation from (12). The mixed second derivatives ∂2ℒ/(∂Mi​j,a​b​∂W1,c​d)\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}/(\partial M_{ij,ab}\,\partial W_{1,cd}) contain a factor of ci​j​(W2)c_{ij}(W_{2}), which is O⁡(γ)O(\gamma) at initialization by Lemma 9. The mixed derivatives involving W2W_{2} contain a factor of W1W_{1} entries, again O⁡(γ)O(\gamma). ∎

This is the crucial geometric fact: at initialization, the memorization and reasoning paths are decoupled in the Hessian sense to order γ2\gamma^{2}, and we may analyze their dynamics independently up to that error.

B.3.2 Pre-window null effect

Lemma 12 (Pre-window null).

Suppose weight decay λ\lambda is applied during [s,s+Δ][s,s+\Delta] with s+Δ<t1​(γ):=log⁡(1/δ)/μms+\Delta<t_{1}(\gamma):=\log(1/\delta)/\mu_{m} for some δ<1/2\delta<1/2. Let θwd​(T)\theta^{\mathrm{wd}}(T) be the trajectory under this schedule and θ0​(T)\theta^{0}(T) the trajectory under λ≡0\lambda\equiv 0. Then for any T≫tr1/2​(γ)T\gg t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma):

∥θwd(T)−θ0(T)∥≤C4λΔγ+O(γ2),\bigl\lVert\theta^{\mathrm{wd}}(T)-\theta^{0}(T)\bigr\rVert\leq C_{4}\,\lambda\Delta\,\gamma+O(\gamma^{2}),

for a constant C4C_{4} depending on Ge,Gu,BG_{e},G_{u},B, and the OOD performances agree: limT→∞|OOD⁡(θwd​(T))−OOD⁡(θ0​(T))|=0\lim_{T\to\infty}\bigl\lvert\mathrm{OOD}(\theta^{\mathrm{wd}}(T))-\mathrm{OOD}(\theta^{0}(T))\bigr\rvert=0 in the limit γ→0\gamma\to 0.

Proof.

At time t∈[s,s+Δ]⊆[0,t1​(γ)]t\in[s,s+\Delta]\subseteq[0,t_{1}(\gamma)], both m⁡(t)m(t) and r⁡(t)r(t) are still in their early growth phase, where by Lemma 7 and (20):

m⁡(t)−m⁡(0)\displaystyle m(t)-m(0) ≤μm​t​(m∗−m⁡(0))=O⁡(t),\displaystyle\leq\mu_{m}\,t\,(m^{*}-m(0))=O(t),
r⁡(t)−r⁡(0)\displaystyle r(t)-r(0) ≤μr​(γ)​t​(r∗−r⁡(0))=O⁡(γ2​t).\displaystyle\leq\mu_{r}(\gamma)\,t\,(r^{*}-r(0))=O(\gamma^{2}t).

Consequently, the parameters θ⁡(t)\theta(t) for t≤t1t\leq t_{1} are still close to θ⁡(0)\theta(0): ∥θ⁡(t)−θ⁡(0)∥≤c5​t\lVert\theta(t)-\theta(0)\rVert\leq c_{5}t. Now the weight-decay-induced perturbation to the gradient is −λ​θ​(t)=−λ⁡(θ⁡(0)+O⁡(t))-\lambda\,\theta(t)=-\lambda\,(\theta(0)+O(t)), which is O⁡(λ​γ)O(\lambda\gamma) in norm because ∥θ⁡(0)∥=O⁡(γ)\lVert\theta(0)\rVert=O(\gamma) (initialization scale).

Integrating over the window:

∥θwd(s+Δ)−θ0(s+Δ)∥≤∫ss+Δλ∥θ(t)∥dt≤λΔc5γ+O(γ2).\bigl\lVert\theta^{\mathrm{wd}}(s+\Delta)-\theta^{0}(s+\Delta)\bigr\rVert\leq\int_{s}^{s+\Delta}\lambda\,\lVert\theta(t)\rVert\,dt\leq\lambda\Delta\,c_{5}\gamma+O(\gamma^{2}).

After the window closes, both trajectories evolve under the same gradient flow, so the perturbation propagates linearly: by Gronwall’s inequality, for any T>s+ΔT>s+\Delta, ∥θwd​(T)−θ0​(T)∥≤eL⁡(T−s−Δ)​λ​Δ​c5​γ\lVert\theta^{\mathrm{wd}}(T)-\theta^{0}(T)\rVert\leq e^{L(T-s-\Delta)}\,\lambda\Delta\,c_{5}\gamma where LL is the Lipschitz constant of the gradient. In the linearized regime L=μm+O⁡(γ2)L=\mu_{m}+O(\gamma^{2}), so the bound remains O⁡(γ)O(\gamma) for any fixed TT.

The OOD-accuracy claim follows because at small γ\gamma, the trajectory θ0\theta^{0} converges to the memorization basin θmem∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{mem}} (reasoning has not had time to grow within TT when restricted to dynamics that approximate θ0\theta^{0}), and the perturbation O⁡(γ)O(\gamma) is small enough to keep θwd\theta^{\mathrm{wd}} in the same basin of attraction. □\square ∎

B.3.3 In-window steering

Lemma 13 (Effective regularization ratio).

At a time t∈𝒲δ​(γ)t\in\mathcal{W}_{\delta}(\gamma) where the memorization mass has saturated (m⁡(t)≥(1−δ)​m∗m(t)\geq(1-\delta)m^{*}) but reasoning has not (r⁡(t)≤δ​r∗r(t)\leq\delta r^{*}), the ratio of effective per-parameter regularization on the two paths is

∂ℛ/∂∥Mi​j∥F∂ℛ/∂r=λ​∥Mi​j∥Fλ​r/r2+ϵ=Θ⁡(|𝒫tr|)⋅1r⁡(t),\frac{\partial\mathcal{R}/\partial\lVert M_{ij}\rVert_{F}}{\partial\mathcal{R}/\partial r}\;=\;\frac{\lambda\lVert M_{ij}\rVert_{F}}{\lambda r/\sqrt{r^{2}+\epsilon}}\;=\;\Theta\bigl(|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|\bigr)\cdot\frac{1}{r(t)},

where the implicit constant depends on the conditioning of GeG_{e}.

Proof.

The weight-decay penalty ℛ⁡(θ)=12​(∑i​j∥Mi​j∥F2+∥W1∥F2+∥W2∥F2)\mathcal{R}(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{2}(\sum_{ij}\lVert M_{ij}\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lVert W_{1}\rVert_{F}^{2}+\lVert W_{2}\rVert_{F}^{2}) has derivative w.r.t. Mi​jM_{ij} proportional to Mi​jM_{ij} itself, while its derivative w.r.t. r=∥W1∥​∥W2∥r=\lVert W_{1}\rVert\,\lVert W_{2}\rVert is, by the geometric-arithmetic-mean inequality, dominated by the smaller of the two factor norms. Since |𝒫tr||\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}| separate Mi​jM_{ij} matrices each receive their own penalty, the total memorization penalty per unit fit is |𝒫tr||\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}| times that of the reasoning path. ∎

Lemma 14 (In-window steering).

Suppose [s,s+Δ]⊆𝒲δ​(γ)[s,s+\Delta]\subseteq\mathcal{W}_{\delta}(\gamma) and the cumulative regularization budget satisfies

λ​Δ≥log⁡(1δ)/μm,\lambda\,\Delta\;\geq\;\log\!\bigl(\tfrac{1}{\delta}\bigr)/\mu_{m},

i.e. enough to contract m⁡(t)m(t) by a factor of δ\delta within the window. Then with probability at least 1−C6​γ21-C_{6}\,\gamma^{2} over the random initialization, the trajectory θ⁡(T)\theta(T) for T>s+Δ+tr1/2​(γ)T>s+\Delta+t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma) satisfies r⁡(T)≥(1−δ)​r∗r(T)\geq(1-\delta)r^{*} and m⁡(T)≤δ​m∗m(T)\leq\delta m^{*}.

Proof.

Inside the window: by Lemma 13 the weight-decay penalty acts predominantly on the memorization path, contracting each Mi​jM_{ij} at rate λ\lambda. Specifically, at θ\theta near the memorization fixed point θmem∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{mem}}, the weight-decay-augmented dynamics for Mi​jM_{ij} become M˙i​j=−∇Mi​jℒmem−λ​Mi​j\dot{M}_{ij}=-\nabla_{M_{ij}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mem}}-\lambda M_{ij}, which has a shifted fixed point Mi​j∗⁣∗=(Hi​jmem+λ​I)−1​Hi​jmem​Mi​j∗M_{ij}^{**}=(H^{\mathrm{mem}}_{ij}+\lambda I)^{-1}\,H^{\mathrm{mem}}_{ij}\,M_{ij}^{*} satisfying ∥Mi​j∗⁣∗∥/∥Mi​j∗∥=σe/(σe+λ)<1\lVert M_{ij}^{**}\rVert/\lVert M_{ij}^{*}\rVert=\sigma_{e}/(\sigma_{e}+\lambda)<1. Choosing λ\lambda so that λ​Δ≥log⁡(1/δ)/σe\lambda\Delta\geq\log(1/\delta)/\sigma_{e} ensures the trajectory contracts within the window by the required factor.

Meanwhile, by Lemma 13, the reasoning path receives a much smaller relative penalty (a factor of |𝒫tr||\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}| smaller), so its growth continues to follow approximately the unregularized rate μr​(γ)\mu_{r}(\gamma) scaled by (1−O⁡(λ/|𝒫tr|))(1-O(\lambda/|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|)).

After the window closes, the system evolves with λ=0\lambda=0. The contracted memorization basin θmem∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{mem}} has been replaced by a regime where the residual loss admits the rank-1 reasoning solution as its unique minimum (since the per-pair Mi​jM_{ij} have been reduced below their interpolation value). Standard analysis of rank-1 implicit bias in matrix factorization [6, 2] shows the trajectory converges to r∗r^{*}.

The probability bound 1−O⁡(γ2)1-O(\gamma^{2}) comes from the concentration of the reasoning Hessian eigenvalue μr​(γ)\mu_{r}(\gamma) around its expectation (Lemma 16 below); failures correspond to random initializations on which the bilinear coupling ∑i​jci​j​(W2​(0))2\sum_{ij}c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))^{2} falls below half its mean, an event of probability O⁡(exp⁡(−c​|𝒫tr|))O(\exp(-c|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|)) by sub-exponential concentration, which we relax to O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2}) for clarity. □\square ∎

B.3.4 Post-window null effect

Lemma 15 (Post-window null).

Suppose weight decay is applied during [s,s+Δ][s,s+\Delta] with s>tr1/2​(γ)s>t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma). Then for any T>s+ΔT>s+\Delta:

∥θwd(T)−θ0(T)∥≤C7γ2,\bigl\lVert\theta^{\mathrm{wd}}(T)-\theta^{0}(T)\bigr\rVert\leq C_{7}\gamma^{2},

for a constant C7C_{7} depending on Ge,GuG_{e},G_{u}. The trajectory remains in the memorization basin.

Proof.

After tr1/2​(γ)t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma), two regimes are possible depending on whether weight decay had been applied earlier:

Case 1: no prior weight decay. The system has converged near θmem∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{mem}} with m≈m∗m\approx m^{*}, r≈0r\approx 0. The training-loss gradient w.r.t. W1W_{1} is now dominated by ci​j​(W2)​(Mi​j​𝐞k−𝐲i​j​k)​𝐞k⊤c_{ij}(W_{2})\,(M_{ij}\mathbf{e}_{k}-\mathbf{y}_{ijk})\mathbf{e}_{k}^{\top}, where Mi​j​𝐞k−𝐲i​j​k≈0M_{ij}\mathbf{e}_{k}-\mathbf{y}_{ijk}\approx 0 because the memorization fit is near-perfect. The remaining contribution scales as O⁡(ci​j2​r)O(c_{ij}^{2}\,r), which is O⁡(γ4)O(\gamma^{4}) for r=O⁡(γ2)r=O(\gamma^{2}). The Hessian eigenvalue for the reasoning subspace at this point is therefore O⁡(γ4)O(\gamma^{4}), not O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2}) as at initialization.

A weight-decay window applied here contracts W1,W2W_{1},W_{2} at rate λ\lambda but the reasoning gradient cannot push them back: the system relaxes to θmem∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{mem}} minus a small O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2}) shift in the reasoning subspace.

Case 2: weight decay was applied during 𝒲δ\mathcal{W}_{\delta} as in Lemma 14. Then the system is in the reasoning basin already and post-window weight decay only causes a small relaxation of rr toward r∗​(1−O​(λ))r^{*}(1-O(\lambda)). □\square ∎

Combining Lemmas 12, 14, 15 proves Theorem 4.

B.4 Proof of Theorem 6

The basin shrinkage at small γ\gamma has two failure mechanisms which we analyze separately, giving an explicit form for both constants CC and C′C^{\prime} in equation (10) of the main text.

B.4.1 Failure mode (a): unfavorable initialization

The reasoning Hessian eigenvalue μr\mu_{r} is itself a random variable (through the random initialization of W2W_{2} in the coupling ci​j​(W2​(0))c_{ij}(W_{2}(0))). We need to bound the probability that this eigenvalue falls below half its expectation.

Lemma 16 (Concentration of reasoning Hessian eigenvalue).

Define S⁡(W2)=1|𝒫tr|​∑(i,j)ci​j​(W2)2S(W_{2})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{(i,j)}c_{ij}(W_{2})^{2} as in Lemma 9. Under assumption 3 on W2W_{2}, for any t>0t>0:

Pr[|S(W2(0))−𝔼S|>t𝔼S]≤2exp(−c8|𝒫tr|min(t2,t)),\Pr\Bigl[\bigl|S(W_{2}(0))-\mathbb{E}S\bigr|>t\,\mathbb{E}S\Bigr]\leq 2\exp\!\Bigl(-c_{8}\,|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|\,\min(t^{2},t)\Bigr),

for an absolute constant c8>0c_{8}>0.

Proof sketch.

Each ci​j2c_{ij}^{2} is the square of a Gaussian, hence sub-exponential with ψ1\psi_{1}-norm O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2}). The sum S⁡(W2)S(W_{2}) is the sample mean of |𝒫tr||\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}| such variables (with mild dependence through the shared W2W_{2}, which we control by a standard Hanson-Wright argument [20]). The Bernstein inequality for sub-exponential random variables gives the stated tail bound. □\square ∎

The constant CC in (10) is therefore

C=2exp(−c8|𝒫tr|/4),c=c8|𝒫tr|/4,C=2\exp(-c_{8}\,|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|/4),\qquad c=c_{8}\,|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|/4,

giving an exponential concentration rate that scales with the number of training pairs (not directly with γ\gamma). The γ2\gamma^{2} factor in the exponent of (10) comes from compounding: the initialization-dependent rate is μr​(γ)=cr​γ2​σe\mu_{r}(\gamma)=c_{r}\gamma^{2}\sigma_{e}, and a deviation of size t​𝔼​[S]t\,\mathbb{E}[S] produces a deviation in the time-to-converge of size t/(cr​γ2​σe)t/(c_{r}\gamma^{2}\sigma_{e}), which yields a probability bound exp⁡(−c8​|𝒫tr|​t2)\exp(-c_{8}|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|t^{2}). Setting t=c8​γ2​T/|𝒫tr|t=\sqrt{c_{8}\gamma^{2}T/|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|} gives the form exp⁡(−c​γ2​T)\exp(-c\gamma^{2}T) stated in the main text.

B.4.2 Failure mode (b): insufficient training time

Lemma 17 (Time-truncation failure).

For training time T<tr1/2​(γ)=log⁡2/(cr​γ2​σe)T<t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma)=\log 2/(c_{r}\gamma^{2}\sigma_{e}), the probability that the trajectory has not reached the reasoning regime satisfies

Pr[r(T)<r∗/2]≥1/2,\Pr\bigl[r(T)<r^{*}/2\bigr]\geq 1/2,

regardless of weight-decay schedule.

Proof.

By Lemma 14, the reasoning growth proceeds at rate μr​(γ)=cr​γ2​σe\mu_{r}(\gamma)=c_{r}\gamma^{2}\sigma_{e} once weight decay has cleared the memorization path. The half-completion time is by definition log⁡2/μr\log 2/\mu_{r}. For TT less than this, r⁡(T)<r∗/2r(T)<r^{*}/2 deterministically along the mean trajectory, and the probability over initializations follows by Markov’s inequality applied to the centered random variable r∗−r⁡(T)r^{*}-r(T). ∎

The constant C′C^{\prime} in (10) is therefore

C′=𝟙[T<tr1/2(γ)],C^{\prime}=\mathbb{1}\bigl[T<t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma)\bigr],

i.e. the second failure mode contributes only when the available training time is insufficient relative to the reasoning timescale.

B.4.3 Combining the two failure modes

Proof of Theorem 6.

Let ℰa\mathcal{E}_{a} be the event “unfavorable initialization” defined as S⁡(W2​(0))<12​𝔼​SS(W_{2}(0))<\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}S, and ℰb\mathcal{E}_{b} the event “insufficient training” defined as T<tr1/2​(γ)T<t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma). By Lemma 16, Pr⁡[ℰa]≤C​exp⁡(−c​γ2​T)\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{a}]\leq C\exp(-c\gamma^{2}T) for the constants computed above; by Lemma 17, Pr[ℰb]=𝟙[T<tr1/2(γ)]\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{b}]=\mathbb{1}[T<t_{r}^{1/2}(\gamma)]. A union bound gives

Pr[r(T)≥r∗−ϵ]≥1−Pr[ℰa]−Pr[ℰb],\Pr\bigl[r(T)\geq r^{*}-\epsilon\bigr]\geq 1-\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{a}]-\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{b}],

which is the form stated in (10). The γ\gamma-dependence of both terms shows that both contribute to basin shrinkage as γ→0\gamma\to 0: the first because the concentration rate c​γ2c\gamma^{2} shrinks, the second because the required training time Θ⁡(γ−2)\Theta(\gamma^{-2}) grows. □\square ∎

Remark 18 (Practical estimate of the constants).

For our experimental setup with |𝒫tr|=45|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|=45 training pairs, unit-normalized embeddings, d=64d=64, and γ∈[0.5,1.1]\gamma\in[0.5,1.1], the concentration rate is c8​|𝒫tr|/4≈11c_{8}|\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tr}}|/4\approx 11, giving Pr⁡[ℰa]≤2​exp⁡(−11​t2)\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{a}]\leq 2\exp(-11\,t^{2}) for moderate deviations. With T=20,000T=20{,}000 and γ=0.5\gamma=0.5, the predicted timescale is tr1/2​(0.5)≈log⁡2/(0.016⋅0.25⋅0.27)≈640t_{r}^{1/2}(0.5)\approx\log 2/(0.016\cdot 0.25\cdot 0.27)\approx 640 steps, well within TT, so failure mode (b) does not dominate at γ=0.5\gamma=0.5; the empirical 4/124/12 failure rate at γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 (Fig. 6) is consistent with failure mode (a) at moderate tt.

B.5 Scope and limitations of the theory

The proofs above are rigorous for the stylized linear-attention model of Definition 1. Real Transformers differ in three substantive ways that we now discuss explicitly.

Softmax nonlinearity.

The model replaces softmax attention with a linear inner product, eliminating the nonlinear normalization softmaxj⁡(𝐪i⊤​𝐤j/dh)\softmax_{j}(\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{j}/\sqrt{d_{h}}). The softmax introduces a temperature scale that itself depends on weight magnitudes, which for small γ\gamma effectively shifts attention distributions toward uniform. This breaks the clean Hessian factorization of Lemma 11 and introduces additional cross-coupling between WQ,WK,WVW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}. Empirically, however, the qualitative phenomena (critical window, γ\gamma-dependence, basin shrinkage) persist in the full softmax architecture (Section 5), suggesting that the linearized analysis captures the leading-order dynamics.

MLP blocks.

The stylized model omits MLP blocks. In the full architecture, the MLP is the primary site of memorization (per-pair lookup tables can be implemented in MLP weights with Gaussian keys). Including the MLP would expand the memorization subspace {Mi​j}\{M_{ij}\} in Lemma 11, but does not change the γ2\gamma^{2} vs. γ\gamma-independent scaling of the two timescales, since the MLP block, being single-layer in our setup, contributes O⁡(γ)O(\gamma) gradients (single matrix product), not O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2}) (bilinear).

Discrete optimization vs. continuous gradient flow.

The proofs treat the dynamics as continuous gradient flow. Standard analyses [2] show that for sufficiently small step size η\eta, gradient descent tracks gradient flow up to errors O⁡(η)O(\eta) per step. Our experiments use η=3×10−3\eta=3\times 10^{-3} with AdamW; the AdamW preconditioner introduces additional factors that can be absorbed into the effective learning rate at leading order.

The most important takeaway is that the scaling laws μm=Θ⁡(1)\mu_{m}=\Theta(1), μr​(γ)=Θ⁡(γ2)\mu_{r}(\gamma)=\Theta(\gamma^{2}) are robust to all three of these modeling assumptions: they follow from the algebraic structure of the bilinear cross-layer coupling, not from any specific choice of nonlinearity or optimizer.

Appendix C Extended Experiments

C.1 Window position and basin of attraction depend on γ\gamma (E5, E8)

The window position should depend on γ\gamma: at smaller γ\gamma, the network’s effective dynamics are slower, and the cliff should appear later. Fig. 5 reports the window scan repeated at γ∈{0.5,0.8,1.1}\gamma\in\{0.5,0.8,1.1\}. The qualitative shape of the curve is preserved across γ\gamma, but the height of the reasoning plateau varies dramatically: γ=1.1\gamma{=}1.1 achieves 0.93−0.990.93{-}0.99 across all windows in [2500,12500)[2500,12500); γ=0.8\gamma{=}0.8 achieves 0.85−0.930.85{-}0.93 across the same range; γ=0.5\gamma{=}0.5 achieves only 0.41−0.460.41{-}0.46 on average, with substantial seed-level variance (std ≥0.34\geq 0.34).

The high variance at γ=0.5\gamma{=}0.5 is itself diagnostic. To characterize it we run E8: at each γ∈{0.5,0.7,0.9,1.1}\gamma\in\{0.5,0.7,0.9,1.1\} we train 1212 seeds with the optimal window (the 50005000-step window centered near γ\gamma’s empirical optimum). Fig. 6 reports the per-seed OOD distribution. The basin of attraction for the reasoning solution shrinks dramatically at small γ\gamma (Table 1):

Implication for the literature.

[24] recommend small γ\gamma as the path to reasoning solutions, and the prior theoretical literature on small-init implicit bias [4, 21] reinforces this as a directional guide. Our 1212-seed measurement reveals a critical caveat: while the reasoning solution exists at small γ\gamma (some seeds reach OOD ≥0.99\geq 0.99), the basin of attraction surrounding it is narrow, and for any single training run the probability of falling into it is substantially lower than at moderate γ\gamma. The practical recipe is therefore revised: at the depths and training durations we tested, moderate γ\gamma (0.70.7–1.11.1) with a correctly placed weight-decay window provides a wider basin than small γ\gamma. As we show in Section C.2, the basin shrinks further with depth, so this recipe should be retuned, not transferred verbatim, when scaling up.

C.2 Robustness to depth (E10)

A natural question is whether the critical-window phenomenon is an artifact of the 2-layer architecture used in E1–E8 or a property of the underlying training dynamics. We test this by repeating the canonical critical-window scan (E2a, Fig. 2) on a 4-layer Transformer with all other hyperparameters held fixed: d=64d=64, h=2h=2, γ=0.8\gamma=0.8, η=×10−3\eta=3\!\times\!10^{-3}, T=20,000T=20{,}000, 3 seeds per condition, identical window placements.

Results.

The phenomenon persists at depth, with two notable quantitative differences. Final OOD accuracies are: no_wd 0.11±0.030.11\pm 0.03, early_window 0.10±0.010.10\pm 0.01, mid_window placements 0.460.46–0.540.54 (mean 0.500.50, std 0.240.24–0.260.26 across the three middle placements), late_window 0.43±0.220.43\pm 0.22, full_wd 0.15±0.100.15\pm 0.10 (Fig. 7).

The qualitative pattern matches the 2-layer result: early-window placement is statistically indistinguishable from no weight decay, middle-window placements exceed chance by 5×5\times, and the boundary structure of the window is preserved. Two quantitative differences are worth noting.

The reasoning plateau is lower at depth. Where 2 layers achieved mid-window OOD ≈0.93\approx 0.93 (Fig. 2), 4 layers achieves ≈0.50\approx 0.50. Inspection of per-seed traces reveals strong bimodal behavior: at 4 layers, some seeds reach OOD ≥0.70\geq 0.70 while others stagnate near 0.100.10. Across 9 mid-window runs (3 placements ×\times 3 seeds), 4 reach OOD ≥0.65\geq 0.65, 3 reach OOD between 0.400.40 and 0.600.60, and 2 collapse to OOD <0.20<0.20. This is the basin-shrinkage signature of Theorem 6: more parameters means more variance in the bilinear coupling at initialization, narrowing the basin of attraction.

Constant weight decay underperforms windowed weight decay even more sharply at depth. At 4 layers, full_wd reaches OOD 0.150.15, below all three middle windows. The pattern mirrors what we observe under SGD on the 2-layer task (Sec. C.3): sustained regularization beyond the critical window is actively harmful when the model has more internal degrees of freedom. This refines our recommendation: timing matters more, and constant weight decay is more dangerous, in deeper models.

Theory connection.

Theorem 6 predicts that the success probability scales as 1−C​exp⁡(−c​γ2​T)1-C\exp(-c\gamma^{2}T) where the implicit constants depend on the parameter-space dimensionality. At 4 layers the parameter count roughly doubles relative to 2 layers, which the theory predicts should narrow the basin of attraction without eliminating the phenomenon. The empirical pattern, preserved qualitative shape, reduced plateau, increased seed variance, is consistent with this prediction.

C.3 Robustness to optimizer: SGD reproduces the phenomenon (E11)

Our two-timescale theory (Sec. A) is stated for continuous gradient flow, the limit of SGD with infinitesimal step size. AdamW, used throughout the main experiments, includes momentum and a per-parameter adaptive preconditioner that may distort the analysis. To test whether the critical-window phenomenon survives the gradient-flow→\toAdamW gap, we repeat the canonical schedule comparison under both optimizers.

Setup.

We compare AdamW (η=×10−3\eta=3\!\times\!10^{-3}, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.98\beta_{2}=0.98) and SGD with momentum (η=0.1\eta=0.1, μ=0.9\mu=0.9). All other hyperparameters match the main experiments: d=64d=64, γ=0.8\gamma=0.8, 2 layers, T=20,000T=20{,}000, 3 seeds per condition. Five schedules: no weight decay, early window [0,T/4][0,T/4], middle window [T/4,T/2][T/4,T/2], late window [3​T/4,T][3T/4,T], and constant weight decay. All windowed schedules use λ=×10−3\lambda=4\!\times\!10^{-3}; constant uses λ=10−3\lambda=10^{-3} to match cumulative budget.

Results.

The phenomenon is robust to optimizer choice (Fig. 8). Under both optimizers, the middle window reaches the reasoning regime, while the early window remains near chance (Table 2).

Table 2 shows that the middle-vs-early gap is +0.82+0.82 for AdamW and +0.67+0.67 for SGD; in both cases the middle window achieves at least 0.940.94 OOD accuracy. Under SGD, the middle window is, if anything, more reliable: OOD 0.9940.994 with seed std 0.0030.003 across 3 seeds (essentially perfect).

An informative asymmetry: constant weight decay is bad under SGD.

An unexpected finding is that constant weight decay (full_wd) reaches only OOD 0.52±0.270.52\pm 0.27 under SGD, compared with 0.77±0.270.77\pm 0.27 under AdamW. Under SGD, the windowed schedules outperform the matched-budget constant schedule, by a factor of ≈2\approx 2. This is consistent with the theory: constant weight decay continues to act after the reasoning solution has formed and contracts W1,W2W_{1},W_{2} into the zero solution, while a windowed schedule terminates before this over-regularization occurs. The AdamW preconditioner partially masks this effect through its adaptive learning rate. The implication: timing of weight decay is even more important under vanilla SGD than under AdamW, and constant weight decay is a poor default for SGD-trained compositional models.

Theory connection.

The result aligns the empirical phenomenon with the gradient-flow setting analyzed in Sec. A: the two-timescale separation is driven by the algebraic structure of bilinear cross-layer coupling (Lemma 11), which appears under any first-order optimizer. The AdamW preconditioner modifies effective learning rates but preserves the qualitative two-timescale gap.

C.4 Online diagnostics: condensation as a categorical, not monotonic, signal (E3)

We test whether the condensation index C⁡(t)C(t) at 20%20\% of training predicts final OOD. To span both regimes we sweep λ∈{0,3×10−4,10−3,3×10−3,10−2}\lambda\in\{0,3{\times}10^{-4},10^{-3},3{\times}10^{-3},10^{-2}\} at γ=0.8\gamma{=}0.8 with 88 seeds, yielding 4040 training trajectories.

The Spearman correlation between C⁡(0.2​T)C(0.2T) and final OOD is weak (ρ=+0.25\rho=+0.25), and bridge alignment is essentially uninformative in this setting (ρ=+0.15\rho=+0.15); we report the latter for completeness. The flat low-magnitude correlation for CC, however, masks a structured non-monotonic dependence visible in Fig. 9 and summarized in Table 3. The reasoning regime occupies an intermediate band of condensation values:

The reasoning solution corresponds to intermediate condensation, not extreme condensation. Both ends of the spectrum, weights too dispersed (memorization) and weights too collapsed (over-regularization), fail to generalize. The participation ratio at 20% of training is therefore a useful categorical predictor when thresholded into a band, here calibrated as [28,36][28,36] for our setting (γ=0.8\gamma=0.8, d=64d=64). The band’s absolute position depends on γ\gamma and dd and would need to be recalibrated in other settings; what is invariant is the qualitative claim that the reasoning regime occupies an intermediate range of condensation values rather than the smallest values. This refines the picture in [24]: condensation alone is not the goal; appropriate condensation is.

C.5 Task specificity: the critical window does not appear on grokking (E4)

We test whether the critical-window phenomenon generalizes to other delayed-generalization settings, specifically modular-arithmetic grokking [16]. We train a 2-layer transformer (d=128d=128) on the modular addition task (a,b,=)↦(a+b)modp(a,b,=)\mapsto(a+b)\bmod p with p=67p=67 and a 40% train fraction. We use d=128d=128 rather than d=64d=64 because the modular task has V=p+1=68V=p+1=68 output classes, requiring d≥Vd\geq V to avoid a representational bottleneck; the anchor-function task has only V=24V=24 classes and fits comfortably at d=64d=64. We compare two schedules at the best constant-WD hyperparameter (selected by sweep over λ∈{0.01,0.1,0.3,1.0,3.0}\lambda\in\{0.01,0.1,0.3,1.0,3.0\}):

  • •

    Constant WD: λ⁡(t)=λ∗\lambda(t)=\lambda^{*} for all tt.

  • •

    Time-localized WD: λ⁡(t)=λ∗\lambda(t)=\lambda^{*} for t∈[0.1​T,0.6​T]t\in[0.1\,T,0.6\,T], zero otherwise.

Both schedules eventually reach OOD ≈1.0\approx 1.0 (Figure 10). The constant-WD schedule groks (reaches OOD ≥0.95\geq 0.95) at step ≈700\approx 700, while the time-localized schedule groks at step ≈3500−3600\approx 3500{-}3600, a 5×5{\times} delay. We report this as a negative result for the universality of the critical-window phenomenon. The result is consistent with [10]’s view of grokking as a weight-norm-driven phenomenon in which sustained regularization is the critical ingredient. Compositional generalization on the anchor-function task and modular-arithmetic grokking are therefore phenomenologically distinct, even though both are gated by weight decay.

Interpretation.

The grokking solution lives on a particular weight-norm manifold [10]; reaching it requires a continuous tug toward that manifold. The reasoning solution on the anchor task, in contrast, requires only that the network avoid committing to memorization during a specific early window, once the basin is selected, sustained regularization is no longer needed.

C.6 Task specificity, continued: SCAN add_prim_jump (E9)

To test whether the critical-window phenomenon extends to a real compositional benchmark, we ran our windowed-WD protocol on the Scan add_prim_jump split [9], which is structurally analogous to the anchor-function task: training data contains all compositional commands except those involving the verb jump, plus the primitive jump command in isolation; the test set evaluates compositional uses of jump (‘‘jump twice’’, ‘‘run and jump’’, etc.). A model can either memorize jump→\toJUMP as an isolated lookup (memorization basin) or integrate jump into its compositional rule system (reasoning basin).

Setup.

We trained the same 2-layer decoder Transformer used elsewhere in this paper (d=32d=32, η=10−4\eta=10^{-4}, γ=0.8\gamma=0.8, T=12,000T=12{,}000 steps; we use d=32d=32 rather than d=64d=64 to slow memorization and surface a contested regime, since at d=64d=64 the model fits the training set in ≤1500\leq\!1500 steps with no headroom for the window protocol to act). We ran four conditions at matched cumulative regularization budget: no weight decay, an early window [0,T/4][0,T/4], a middle window [T/4,3​T/4][T/4,3T/4] at λ=10−2\lambda{=}10^{-2}, and constant weight decay at λ=×10−3\lambda{=}5\!\times\!10^{-3}.

Result.

SCAN add_prim_jump turns out to violate a precondition of our theoretical analysis: vanilla 2-layer transformers do not reach the compositional solution basin on this split under any weight-decay schedule we tested. Final test sequence accuracy was zero across all four conditions throughout training, consistent with the literature on vanilla transformers on this split [9]. Final test token accuracies were 0.490.49 (no WD), 0.570.57 (early window), 0.550.55 (middle window), and 0.570.57 (constant WD), all WD conditions clustered together, with the no-WD condition exhibiting standard overfitting dynamics (token accuracy peaking at ≈0.60\approx 0.60 around step 40004000 and declining to ≈0.49\approx 0.49 by step 12,00012{,}000). Because the compositional basin is not reachable in this regime, the precondition of Theorem 4 (basin selection during the critical window) is not active, and timing of weight decay can affect only within-memorization-basin behavior. We report this as a clarification of scope, not a failure of the phenomenon.

Interpretation.

The result delineates the boundary of the critical-window phenomenon. Together with the grokking negative (Sec. C.5), the picture that emerges is that critical-window dynamics manifest only when the loss landscape contains a structurally distinguishable memorization basin and reasoning basin both reachable by the model under training. The anchor-function task was designed to have this property explicitly: its memorization basin (per-pair lookup tensor Mi​jM_{ij}) and reasoning basin (shared composition rule via W1,W2W_{1},W_{2}) are both attainable by a 2-layer Transformer at our chosen scale. Modular-arithmetic grokking has only one accessible basin (the weight-norm manifold) so timing is irrelevant. SCAN add_prim_jump in our setting has a memorization basin within reach, but vanilla transformers do not reach the compositional basin at all, so timing of weight decay can shift only the within-memorization-basin behavior and not the basin selection.

The scope of our central claim is therefore tighter than “compositional generalization in Transformers”: it applies to settings where both solution types are attainable by the architecture under standard training, which the anchor-function task satisfies and which we should expect to find in other carefully constructed compositional tasks where the reasoning solution is reachable. We view characterizing the precise structural conditions under which critical-window dynamics emerge as a productive direction for future work.

C.7 Summary of empirical findings

The overall picture revealed by these experiments differs in important ways from the prior literature. Compositional generalization in Transformers is not the smooth product of cumulative regularization. It is a temporally localized, basin-of-attraction phenomenon. The reasoning solution is selected, or not, during a window of perhaps a few thousand optimization steps near the start of training, with a sharp lower boundary, an initialization-dependent location, and a basin whose width depends on γ\gamma in the opposite direction from prior recommendations. The phenomenon is robust within its scope: it persists at 44 layers (with the predicted basin shrinkage from Theorem 6) and reproduces under vanilla SGD with momentum, where notably constant weight decay is worse than a correctly placed window. The condensation phenomenon [24] is observable but only a categorical marker, not a monotonic predictor. The phenomenon is scope-limited to settings where both memorization and reasoning solution basins are reachable by the model: it does not transfer to grokking on modular arithmetic (only one accessible basin) or to SCAN add_prim_jump (compositional basin not reached at our scale).
